$comment: Board subsystem: fabrication, soldering, population, test and phototooling of the C64 ASSY 250407 mainboard. Shared ids referenced: metal.copper, metal.tin, metal.lead, chem.silane, chem.ferric-chloride, chem.photoresist, chem.rosin, chem.solder, chem.ethanol, facility.electricity, facility.water, facility.nitrogen.

roots.name: C64 mainboard ASSY 250407 - bare double-sided FR-4 board
roots.description: The unpopulated logic board of a 1983 Commodore 64. A 1.6 mm two-layer epoxy-glass laminate about 390 x 180 mm carrying 35 um copper on both faces, roughly 1200 unplated through-holes for component leads, NO plated-through holes and NO vias at all, green epoxy solder mask on both sides and a white screen-printed legend. Made by an outside printed-circuit-board house, not by Commodore.
roots.note: The board cost is the era figure quoted for the C64 printed-circuit board. A verified reverse-engineered copy of the Rev. B layout contains exactly zero vias, so no layer change goes through a plated barrel anywhere on this board.

children.name: FR-4 copper-clad laminate panel, 1.6 mm
children.description: The structural core of the board: woven E-glass cloth impregnated with a brominated epoxy resin, sandwiched between two 35 um copper foils. It leaves the laminate mill as a rigid panel roughly 1.2 x 2.4 m which the PCB house cuts into working blanks.

facts.label: Core
facts.value: approx. 1.5 mm woven E-glass in brominated epoxy

children.name: Woven E-glass cloth
children.description: Continuous glass filaments woven into a plain-weave cloth that becomes the mechanical skeleton of the laminate. In 1983 the cloth would be roughly 0.1-0.2 mm thick, woven from yarn of about 9-22 tex with 8-18 filaments per centimetre. It is the structural, not the dielectric, member of the board.

children.name: Air-jet or rapier weaving
children.description: Warp and weft yarn are interlaced on a loom. Air-jet looms dominate because they run fast with few picks per inch; rapier looms use a rapier to carry the weft. Some cloth for laminate is stitched rather than woven, which is cheaper and adequate for reinforcement.

children.name: Glass yarn
children.description: Hundreds of continuous filaments twisted together into one yarn, then wound onto a package for the loom. Sizing holds the filaments in place so they do not fuzz or separate.

children.name: Continuous E-glass fibre
children.description: The elementary filament of the reinforcement, drawn from molten glass. E-glass is a borosilicate/aluminosilicate carrying 15-19 % of non-glass oxides, mainly boron and lime, which lower the melting point enough for cheap fine-diameter drawing.

children.name: Bushing filament drawing
children.description: Molten glass is fed to a platinum-rhodium bushing plate perforated with hundreds to thousands of 4-9 um holes and pulled downward at enormous speed. Surface tension, not a die, forms each filament. The fibres gather into a ribbon, are cooled and wound.

children.name: Glass batch (frit)
children.description: A dry blend of silica sand, limestone or dolomite, and boron compounds, with a trace of carbon black so the glass comes out faintly green rather than water-clear. Melting the batch is what feeds the bushing.

children.name: High-purity silica sand
children.description: Low-iron, low-alumina quartz sand, the main glass former. Fibre-grade sand must be very clean, so deposits are washed, floated and acid-leached before melting. This is the terminal raw material of the whole glass chain.

children.name: Sand purification (beneficiation)
children.description: Washing, density separation and flotation remove heavy mineral and clay impurities; an acid leach removes iron, which would otherwise darken the glass. Drying and sieving follow.

children.name: Quartz sand / sandstone deposit
children.description: Weathered quartz grains from unconsolidated deposits or friable sandstone, dug and screened. This is where the board's glass, and therefore a large fraction of its mass, begins as a mineral taken out of the ground.

children.name: Limestone / dolomite
children.description: Adds lime and magnesia to E-glass, lowering the melt temperature and improving the chemical durability of the drawn fibre.

children.name: Boron oxide compounds (colemanite, borax)
children.description: B2O3 lowers the working temperature of the melt, which is what makes fine-diameter drawing practical on ordinary platinum-rhodium equipment.

children.name: Glass melting furnace and bushing
children.description: A regenerative gas furnace melts the batch to a red-hot glass at roughly 1400-1600 deg C, with a nickel-alloy bushing plate riding on the sump. Fuel is almost always natural gas or oil.
children.note: Capital-intensive, but far less so than a semiconductor fab; glass plants of this size existed in the hundreds worldwide by the early 1980s.

children.name: Sizing and binder on the fibre
children.description: Fresh glass fibre is slippery and fragile. Filaments are coated while hot with a thin organosilane sizing plus a film-former such as starch or PVA that holds the ribbon together and stops the yarn fuzzing. For laminate the silane is chosen to form the chemical bond to the epoxy; that interface is the classic site of delamination failure.

children.name: Organosilane coupling agent
children.description: A bifunctional molecule with an alkoxy end that bonds to the glass surface and a reactive organic end that copolymerises with the epoxy. It is the molecular glue that turns a loose glass cloth into a chemically bonded laminate, and it is what makes copper-to-glass peel strength measurable.

children.name: Flame-drawn fibre (roving)
children.description: The cheaper alternative to bushing fibre: glass is remelted in a small furnace and blown through a plate with a few larger holes into 20-30 um fibres. Coarser, so it is used as a surface mat or chopped strand, not as the woven reinforcement itself.
children.note: Some 1980s copper-clad laminate used a thin woven cloth with a flame-drawn mat for extra thickness and better resin flow.

children.name: Brominated DGEBA epoxy resin
children.description: The diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A blended with a brominated epoxy co-resin so the cured laminate self-extinguishes. That blend is the FR in FR-4. This is the board's dielectric and its flame-retardant system, and it is where almost all of the board's non-glass, non-metal mass ends up.

facts.label: Cured glass transition
facts.value: approx. 135-150 deg C for period FR-4

children.name: Bisphenol A backbone
children.description: Condensed from two molecules of phenol with acetone under acid catalysis. This is the reaction that makes the epoxy a thermoset rather than a thermoplastic, and it is the point where petrochemical aromatics enter a material people imagine as 'plastic'.

children.name: Phenol
children.description: Aromatic feedstock for bisphenol A. The cumene process alkylates benzene with propylene to cumene, oxidises it to cumene hydroperoxide, then cleaves with sulfuric acid to give phenol and acetone together.

children.name: Cumene and cumene hydroperoxide
children.description: The intermediate whose acid cleavage is the cheapest industrial route to phenol. Benzene plus propylene over phosphoric or sulfuric acid, then air oxidation.

children.name: Benzene
children.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from heavy naphtha or made by catalytic reforming; the universal starting point for the phenol/cumene chain.

children.name: Heavy naphtha
children.description: A mid-boiling petroleum fraction from which benzene is extracted by solvent recovery. Crude oil is the ultimate source.

children.name: Crude oil
children.description: The hydrocarbon mixture pumped out of a sedimentary reservoir that ultimately supplies every aromatic and olefin feedstock on this branch of the tree.

children.name: Petroleum reservoir
children.description: Porous sandstone or fractured carbonate holding crude oil under pressure. Produced through steel casing and perforated liner into a gathering system, often by water or steam injection to hold down the pressure.

children.name: Propylene
children.description: The C3 olefin used both here and for epichlorohydrin. From steam cracking of propane or naphtha, or as a co-product of ethylene.

children.name: Naphtha steam cracker
children.description: Naphtha vapour pyrolysed at 800-900 deg C in coils to make ethylene, propylene and butenes. A high-temperature furnace that is the gateway from crude to the whole plastics chemistry.

children.name: Epichlorohydrin
children.description: Reacts with bisphenol A in aqueous caustic to give the diglycidyl ether liquid that becomes the binder. Made by chlorohydrin reaction of propylene, then dehydrochlorination.

children.name: Chlorohydrin and dehydrochlorination
children.description: Propylene is chlorohydrinated with hypochlorous acid at low temperature to 1-chloro-2-propanol, which is treated with caustic lime to epichlorohydrin. The caustic also does the ring-opening condensation with bisphenol A.

children.name: Chlorine from brine
children.description: Electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution in diaphragm or membrane cells yields chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. The same caustic soda serves the resin reaction.

children.name: Brine
children.description: Concentrated salt solution evaporated from sea water or saline groundwater.

children.name: Rock salt / evaporite salt
children.description: Halite mined from evaporite deposits or sun-dried from sea water, then dissolved to brine.

children.name: Tetrabromobisphenol-A epoxy co-resin
children.description: The brominated co-resin that gives FR-4 its self-extinguishing behaviour. Bromine radicals released in the gas phase quench the combustion chain, so the laminate passes the UL-94 V-0 burn test.

children.name: Elemental bromine
children.description: A heavy red-brown liquid and the source of the retardant bromine. Made by oxidising bromide-rich brines with chlorine, or by blowing air and steam off seawater treated with chlorine.

children.name: Bromide-rich brine (bittern)
children.description: Mother liquor left from salt manufacture, historically rich enough in bromide to strip bromine from; today also drawn from underground brines.

children.name: Curing agent and cure chemistry
children.description: An amine or anhydride that opens the epoxide rings and cross-links them. The period laminate system was typically a bisphenol-A / diaminodiphenylsulfone blend, which is what set the elevated glass transition temperature of FR-4 sheet.
children.note: The curing agent is not the flame retardant; the retardant is the brominated co-resin. Keep the two straight.

children.name: B-stage prepreg and core sheet
children.description: Glass cloth pulled through epoxy, squeezed between metering nips to a controlled resin content and dried at 120-160 deg C until only partly cross-linked. The result is a dry, slightly tacky, board-like sheet that can be stacked and stored. The residual cure is completed under heat and pressure in the press.
children.note: Roll-to-roll treeline impregnation had largely displaced gap dipping by the early 1980s; it was faster and gave more uniform resin content.

children.name: Hot platen press and the lamination cycle
children.description: A stack of foil, prepreg, core and prepreg is pressed between heated platens. Pressure squeezes out the excess resin and forces it into the weave, and the heat completes the cure. This one step turns loose foil and cloth into a single homogeneous 1.6 mm sheet with copper bonded to both faces.
children.note: Modern high-Tg FR-4 laminates press hotter (200-220 deg C) and harder. Period FR-4 at 175 deg C and 1.4 MPa is the classic cycle.

children.name: Heated platens
children.description: Cast iron platens heated by embedded steam or electric resistance elements and ground flat. The cast iron is the reason a 1980s laminate press can hold a flatness tolerance tighter than anything the component designer asked for.

children.name: Cast iron platen body
children.description: Grey cast iron, machined and surface-ground, chosen for dimensional stability and thermal mass rather than strength.

children.name: Pig iron from blast furnace
children.description: Made by smelting iron ore with coke in a blast furnace, with limestone flux. The same ore and coke that make the platen also make the drill spindles and the wave-solder machine frame.

children.name: Iron ore (hematite/magnetite)
children.description: Run-of-mine ore crushed and concentrated before the blast furnace. The metal backbone of every machine tool on the board line comes from here.

children.name: Iron ore body
children.description: A concentration of iron oxides in banded iron formation or massive hematite, mined by open pit or underground room-and-pillar, then crushed and washed.

children.name: Hydraulic press pack and oil
children.description: Pressure is applied by a hydraulic press pack with multiple heated platens so several laminate books can be pressed at once. The hydraulic oil is refined from crude.

children.name: Hydraulic oil
children.description: A petroleum-derived lubricating fluid circulating through the press. Traced to crude oil like almost every other lubricant on the line.

children.name: Release paper between books
children.description: Bleached or unbleached kraft paper laid between each laminate book so resin does not bond one book to the next and the platen stays clean. Kraft paper is lignin-rich cellulose pulp.
children.note: Also used as the cushion sheet that distributes pressure across the book.

children.name: Press heat source
children.description: Steam coils or electric resistance elements in the platens. Gas- or oil-fired central steam was the norm in a laminate plant of this era.

children.name: Foil bonding and copper-clad laminate
children.description: Treated copper foil, prepreg and core are stacked and press-bonded to give the copper-clad laminate the PCB house buys. The foil is pre-treated so the epoxy keys into it during the press rather than peeling away.
children.note: Commodore pressed none of this. It bought CCL from a merchant laminate plant and did only the imaging, etch, drill and finish itself, at an outside house.

children.name: Copper foil bonding treatment
children.description: ED foil carries a natural fine-pebble surface that grips epoxy. Rolled foil is smooth and must be deliberately roughened or given a nodular peckled treatment so the laminate does not delaminate along the copper interface. This interface is what the peel-strength test measures.
children.note: For a 1 oz consumer board in 1983 ED foil was the normal, cheaper choice; rolled foil was reserved for high-speed or high-temperature laminate.

children.name: Copper foil, 35 um, electro-deposited
children.description: The conductive skin on both faces of the laminate. In 1983 most consumer laminate was clad with electro-deposited foil because it is cheap and its rough surface bonds well to epoxy. Rolled annealed foil was used where thermal or dimensional stability mattered more.
children.note: The copper itself, from cathode through to concentrate, is traced by the metals subsystem; this node only follows the foil-making process as far as the laminate.

children.name: Electrodeposition onto a cathode drum
children.description: Cathode copper is dissolved into a sulfuric acid copper sulfate bath and electroplated onto a slowly rotating titanium or stainless drum. Brighteners and suppressors in the bath control grain so the stripped foil is a dense film rather than a powdery deposit.

children.name: Nodular (peckled) deposition
children.description: The final plating stage deposits fine nodules instead of flat copper. This nodular surface is what gives ED foil its grip on the resin during lamination.

children.name: Drum winding, stripping and slitting
children.description: The drum winds until the foil reaches 35 um, then the foil is peeled off and slit into rolls 1.0-1.4 m wide, the width the laminator needs.

children.name: Dry-film photoresist, negative working
children.description: A dry film about 25-40 um thick, on a PET carrier, laminated onto the copper. Where the artwork film lets UV through, the acrylate resist cross-links and hardens; the hardened areas stand up to the ferric chloride. Everything else dissolves away and the copper under it etches out.

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: negative-working acrylate photopolymer on a polyester carrier

children.note: Period suppliers included Kodak and Dynachem. Dry film was already the default for a two-sided consumer board in 1983; modern shops more often print liquid resist, so the choice has flipped but the principle has not.

children.name: PET carrier film
children.description: The polyester backing the resist is laminated from. Peeled off after lamination and before exposure, leaving the resist on the copper.

children.name: Film lamination of the resist
children.description: The board is baked dry, the film is fed from a spool, heated, and pressed onto the copper by rubber-covered nip rollers. The rubber hardness matters: too hard and it embosses the fragile foil.

facts.label: Control
facts.value: nip rollers and a chill roll to set the film down

children.name: Surface clean and tack-free prep
children.description: Before the resist goes on, the board is degreased and dried so the film lies flat. A tack-free prep was unusual on period boards; wet resist had an easier time of it, which is one reason modern processes moved.
children.note: Wet resist offered the no-prep advantage; dry film offered the thickness control. Dry film won on thickness.

children.name: UV exposure through the artwork film
children.description: The artwork negative is laid against the resist and the board is flood-exposed. In 1983 this was a mercury-vapour or metal-halide lamp in a vacuum-frame exposure unit. Fibre-optic exposure systems that pipe collimated light into a bed of glass rods were spreading through the later 1980s and gave far more even illumination.

facts.label: Exposure time
facts.value: seconds to tens of seconds, set by an integrating light meter

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: film pressed into the resist under vacuum to avoid any air gap

children.note: An air gap between film and resist is the classic cause of a fuzzy, partly-etched trace edge on a two-sided board.

children.name: Vacuum exposure frame
children.description: A hinged platen with a rubber diaphragm. Film and resist are clamped and then evacuated so the film sits hard against the resist with no bubbles and no shadowing.

children.name: Mercury-vapour exposure lamp
children.description: A quartz envelope filled with mercury vapour struck by an arc, rich in the near UV where the acrylate resists are sensitive. Needs a water-cooled jacket and a choke.

children.name: Ferric chloride etching
children.description: The masked laminate goes into warm ferric chloride solution, which dissolves the unmasked copper and leaves traces, pads and ground pour standing. Copper removed along the way is recovered, and the etchant is periodically replenished or dumped.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: ferric chloride, commonly quoted at about 42 deg Baume, warmed to approx. 40-50 deg C

facts.label: Chemistry limit
facts.value: copper in solution poisons the bath, so it is dumped and made fresh

children.note: Period text consistently quotes 42 deg Baume ferric chloride around 45 deg C. Sodium persulfate was a real alternative for some shops. Modern practice is still ferric chloride, but with tighter control and a copper-recovery loop.

children.name: Resist stripping and clean-up
children.description: The cross-linked resist film is dissolved away in a caustic or amine stripper, then the board is rinsed, given a mild acid clean to knock back any last residue, dried, and inspected.

facts.label: Follow-up
facts.value: mild acid clean and deionised rinse

children.name: Routing and outline cutting
children.description: In 1983 the board outline, internal cut-outs and the edge-connector routing slot were milled mechanically on a CNC router with a carbide cutter. Laser routing existed but was not yet the commodity default for a board with no fine geometry.
children.note: Modern high-mix shops use CO2 or UV lasers for routing and depanelising because they need no tooling and leave no router burr; for this board either would be far slower than milling.

children.name: Edge-connector routing slot
children.description: The expansion-port slot is milled so that a thin projecting ear of laminate is left with copper on both faces. That ear is the board edge connector, and its copper is then selectively plated. The slot geometry sets the finger width and spacing that the case connector must mate with.
children.note: Crucially, on the C64 this is a female receptacle on the mainboard, not male fingers: the board carries the socket and the expansion adapter carries the gold fingers. So the C64 mainboard has no board-edge fingers of its own.

children.name: Carbide router cutter
children.description: A tungsten-carbide end mill, often with a diamond-like coating, cutting laminate that is mostly glass fibre. Glass dust is abrasive, so tool life is short and the cutter is changed on a schedule.

children.name: Drilling every component hole
children.description: The board is drilled on a numerical-control drill for every component lead, jumper, jack and mounting hole. Because there are no vias, the drill programme is just a component position list; there is no barrel to plate afterwards.

facts.label: Dominant diameter
facts.value: approx. 1.1 mm for DIP and leaded parts

facts.label: Larger diameters
facts.value: approx. 1.6-4.3 mm for trimmer, fuse and mounting holes

facts.label: Fit
facts.value: hole set slightly oversize so the lead drops in freely for wave soldering

children.note: 0.6 mm leads sat in roughly 0.8-1.0 mm holes. The oversize is deliberate: the wave has to fill the hole and a tight hole makes an unfilled, dry joint.

children.name: NC drill and tool change
children.description: A tape-fed drill head steps through the tool table, swapping bits for the several diameters the board needs, over pinned or vacuum-held fixtures. A bit-management and drill-jig system holds sub-millimetre position accuracy; drill wander is what breaks a fine-pitch DIP row.

children.name: Carbide drill bit
children.description: Tungsten-carbide or high-speed-steel bits, ground and resharpened. Laminated glass plus copper is abrasive and the hole is the one feature that cannot be reworked once drilled wrong.

children.name: How this board changed layer with NO vias
children.description: The most distinctive fact about the C64 mainboard. There are no vias and no plated-through holes. A connection that has to move from the component side to the solder side does it by passing through the hole of a component lead: every resistor, capacitor, diode and DIP pin doubles as a via. Where a layer change was needed with no component available, the board carried a short single-core tinned wire jumper, hand-fitted and hand-soldered after wave soldering.

facts.label: Wire jumpers
facts.value: 2 (E1 solid, E2 dashed on the artwork)

facts.label: What they connect
facts.value: a top-side signal to a bottom-side return

children.note: The two jumpers appear as footprint references E1 and E2 in a verified reverse-engineered copy of the 250407 layout. The saving was real: skipping the barrel plating line removed a whole wet-chemical operation and let the board stay two-sided and cheap. The cost was longer traces and a harder time with high-speed return current.

children.name: Ground pour instead of a ground plane
children.description: With no internal plane layer, the two signal layers carry return current on their own copper, so the layout used wide ground pours and heavy copper wherever return current had to flow. Modern boards solve the same electromagnetic problem with a dedicated plane, which is the main reason vias became universal.

children.name: Surface finish: pads and edge contacts
children.description: After etching the copper is protected, made solderable, and given a wear-resistant finish where it will be touched. On this board, because there are no plated barrels, the finish job is far simpler than on a modern via board.

children.name: HASL solder level on the pads
children.description: Exposed copper is coated in molten solder by carrying the board through a wave or a drag of 63/37 tin-lead and blowing or brushing off the excess, leaving a flat solderable layer that will not corrode. This is the period default for a two-sided consumer board with no vias, and it lines up with the solder the wave machine is already using.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: a few micrometres of tin-lead over copper

facts.label: Bath temperature
facts.value: hot enough to keep the alloy molten, several degrees above 183 deg C

children.note: Modern boards use ENIG, immersion tin or OSP instead; HASL went out of fashion because its coating is soft and its thermal expansion mismatch causes failures in cycling. It was, however, ideal for a board that was going straight into a tin pot.

children.name: Selective plating of the edge contacts
children.description: Only the edge-connector contact surfaces get a hard, wear-resistant metal. The usual route is a nickel underplate followed by electrolytic gold applied through a fountain plater or a selective rack, with everything else masked. Sometimes the entire board is immersion gold-plated instead, which is simpler and gives softer gold.

facts.label: Underplate
facts.value: nickel, commonly electroless with a thin electrolytic strike

facts.label: Gold thickness
facts.value: hard gold, roughly 1-2.5 um for a card-edge finger

facts.label: Gold bath
facts.value: cyanide-based, gold cyanide or gold sulfite

children.note: On the C64 mainboard specifically these contacts are inside the female expansion, user and cassette sockets, so the gold belongs to a purchased connector; the mating plug cards carry the fingers. The plating chemistry is the same either way.

children.name: Selective masking
children.description: The board is plated overall and the gold is stripped from everywhere except the contact surfaces, or the contacts alone are exposed to the bath with the rest of the board shielded by a fountain-plater weir or a plating rack.

children.name: Cyanide gold bath
children.description: Gold dissolves in a cyanide complex with a fine gold anode; the cathode is the board rack. Cyanide plating baths are still the standard because they are stable and fast, and still require the same destruction-and recovery regime.

children.name: Anti-tarnish treatment
children.description: A benzotriazole-type organic protectant is applied to stop the non-plated copper from darkening in storage and handling. Cheap, invisible, and easy to skip until someone notices the boards going brown in the box.

children.name: Plated-barrel line - NOT on this board
children.description: The C64 mainboard skips the entire through-hole plating sequence a via board runs: hole desmear, electroless copper seed, electrolytic copper build, nickel, gold. This node exists to make the absence explicit, because it is a common and wrong assumption about this board.
children.note: Empty branch by design. The 250407 has zero vias and zero plated barrels; anything that puts electroless copper into a C64 mainboard is wrong.

children.name: Epoxy solder mask on both sides
children.description: Green epoxy ink is screen-printed over the whole board with apertures left over every pad and hole. It is the green the C64 has always been. Without it the board shorts from a fingerprint, a solder splash or a screw, and the white legend would disappear under bare copper.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: epoxy, screen-printed through a fine mesh

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: UV or thermal, typically around 150 deg C for half an hour

facts.label: Aperture allowance
facts.value: a little larger than the pad, so pads do not look ringed

children.note: Period inks were solvent-based epoxies cured in infrared or hot-air ovens. Modern liquid solder mask (LPI) is still screen-printed and cured far more cleanly; LPI plus ENIG is now the standard pairing.

children.name: White silkscreen legend and compartment boxes
children.description: Reference designators, block outlines and assembly notes are printed in white epoxy ink over the cured mask and baked. Commodore drew boxes around functional blocks, the so-called compartments, and used extra ink colours in bands and outlines to colour-code regions of the board and mark the television standard.
children.note: Coloured bands mean a second and third screen pass in a different ink, each with its own screen, squeegee pass and cure. This is a real cost and a real time step on the line.

children.name: Screen printing and bake
children.description: A fine-mesh screen coated with photosensitive emulsion is stretched and tensioned over the board, epoxy ink squeegeed through, and the board then baked to cure the ink onto the mask.

children.name: Coloured silkscreen bands
children.description: A separate pass in each extra colour, with its own screen, to draw the colour bands and outlines that mark functional regions and the PAL or NTSC variant. A modern cosmetic imitation of this is a coloured solder mask; in 1983 it was extra ink passes.
children.note: The exact set of colours used on the 250407 has not been confirmed here.

children.name: Electrical test of the bare board
children.description: Before any component goes on, the blank is checked for shorts between nets and for opens in the artwork. In 1983 this was a continuity and insulation-resistance tester plus a careful visual check under a lamp and a loupe; automated optical inspection was available but too expensive to be assumed on every commodity line.
children.note: AOI existed by 1983 but was a line investment. Modern lines AOI every board automatically and add impedance and resistance checks as well.

children.name: Finished bare board, fab no. 250406
children.description: A drilled, etched, stripped, masked, legended and finished blank ready for component insertion. At 1983 commodity prices a two-layer 1.6 mm consumer board of this size cost on the order of one to two dollars.

facts.label: Etch and drill yield
facts.value: typically high; a two-layer board with no vias has few ways to fail

children.note: The $1-2 figure is the era cost quoted for the C64 printed-circuit board.

roots.name: Lead-tin solder and every joint it makes on the board
roots.description: The metallurgical spine of the whole machine. Every joint on the C64 mainboard is made with 63/37 tin-lead alloy activated by rosin flux: about 600 in one pass through a wave-soldering machine, the rest by hand afterwards on the connectors, fuse clips and wire jumpers.

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 183 deg C, a sharp single transition

roots.note: The eutectic was the right choice, and the reason is worth stating: at 63/37 the alloy melts and solidifies at one temperature instead of a mushy range, so a joint leaves the wave already set. 60/40, common for hand work, freezes over a range and gives duller, greyer joints.

children.name: 63/37 tin-lead eutectic
children.description: A true eutectic: solid below 183 deg C, liquid above it, no pasty region in between. That sharpness is what lets a drag-soldered joint finish setting the instant it leaves the wave, and it is why the wave pot and the pad finish are the same alloy.

facts.label: Main weakness
facts.value: creeps under load, especially at elevated temperature

children.name: Tin, 63 % of the alloy
children.description: Tin does the actual joining: it reacts with the copper in the pad to form the intermetallic that holds the joint, and it flows first and wets the joint, which is why a good joint is shiny where the tin pooled.
children.note: Tin's own supply chain, from cassiterite concentrate to refined tin, is traced by the metals subsystem under metal.tin.

children.name: Lead, 37 % of the alloy
children.description: Lead lowers the melting point, widens the working window and suppresses tin whisker growth. It is also soft, creeps, and is a cumulative poison that nobody in a 1983 electronics factory thought about.
children.note: Lead's chain from galena through the sinter and blast furnace to refined bullion is traced by the metals subsystem under metal.lead.

children.name: Antimony and silver additions
children.description: A little antimony hardens the alloy and slows the tin pest; silver is used in higher-temperature solders to slow pad dissolution. General-purpose wave bar in 1983 was usually plain 63/37.
children.note: Whether Commodore specified antimony-bearing bar is not established.

children.name: Cast solder bar and the dross it makes
children.description: Solder arrives at the plant as roughly 0.5-1 kg bars and is dropped into the wave machine's pot. As tin dissolves copper from every pad that passes through the wave, the pot chemistry drifts and a grey oxide sludge called dross accumulates on the surface, which has to be skimmed off or the wave itself is contaminated.

facts.label: Pot capacity
facts.value: tens to hundreds of kg in a production machine

facts.label: Dross
facts.value: tin oxide plus dissolved copper, skimmed off the surface

children.name: Solder wire with a rosin core
children.description: For joints the wave cannot reach, the line uses 0.5-0.8 mm wire with a rosin flux core extruded down the middle. About a quarter of the wire by weight is flux; as the solder melts the flux boils off ahead of it, cleaning the joint just before the tin arrives.

facts.label: Wire gauge
facts.value: approx. 0.5-0.8 mm at this lead pitch

facts.label: Flux core
facts.value: roughly 25 % of wire weight, rosin based

children.name: Drawing the wire from the bar
children.description: Cast bar is hot-worked and cold-drawn through a series of dies to a fine round or rectangular section, with the flux core fed into the tube just before the final pass. The dies are carbide, because tin-lead is abrasive and destroys steel tooling quickly.

children.name: Carbide drawing die
children.description: A tungsten-carbide insert in a steel holder. Carbide is used throughout the solder shop and the board shop, from wire drawing dies to the wave pot's skimmer blade, because nothing softer survives contact with molten tin.

children.name: Tungsten and cobalt in the carbide
children.description: Tungsten comes from wolframite and scheelite concentrates, cobalt from cobalt ore. Both are mined metals, and both are chosen here for one reason only: they do not wear away in molten tin.

children.name: Tungsten ore (wolframite)
children.description: Heavy, dark ore worked for its tungsten content, usually concentrated from alluvial and vein deposits before conversion to ammonium paratungstate and then to the metal.
children.note: In 1980s carbide tooling was increasingly using the far cheaper cemented carbide rather than the older hardened steel; the ore behind it is a genuine dependency of the fabrication process.

children.name: Wolframite ore body
children.description: A vein or alluvial concentration of iron-manganese tungstate, mined by stope or by hydraulic gravel washing and concentrated before the conversion plant. Diggable rock, at the very bottom of a chain that exists only because a die must survive molten tin.

children.name: Rosin flux core
children.description: Sticky pine resin dissolved in alcohol with a mild organic-acid activator. Rosin is not corrosive, and at wave temperature it burns off cleanly, but what is left behind is a sticky, mildly acidic film that has to be cleaned off the board. Its whole job is to displace the oxide film on the copper in the few milliseconds before the solder touches it.
children.note: Rosin flux was still the default in 1983. Low-solids 'no-clean' fluxes that skip the cleaning step existed but were not standard here; the goal was halide-free, not no-clean.

children.name: Colophony (rosin) from pine
children.description: The sticky amber resin tapped from living pine and, in modern supply, distilled from pine stumps. Dissolved in alcohol it is the flux; it is non-corrosive and, crucially, only slightly conductive, which is what keeps a rosin-fluxed board from slowly corroding itself.

children.name: Pine stumps and resin
children.description: Stumps left by logging are chipped and steam-distilled to recover the resin, which is why pine-resin supply for electronics solder is a forestry business and not an agriculture one.

children.name: Abietic acid in the rosin
children.description: The organic acid that gives rosin its mild acidity and its ability to dissolve metal oxides. It is also what makes the residue on an uncleaned board slowly corrosive, which is the whole argument for cleaning after soldering.

children.name: Flux activator (halide-free)
children.description: A small addition of organic acid, chosen to be aggressive against copper oxide but free of ionic halides. An ionic chloride in a flux does a better job of the chemistry and then quietly destroys the board with corrosion under the mask years later, so the halide-free requirement is a deliberate long-term trade.
children.note: Periodic practice was to specify a halide-free (non-ionic) flux and test for it; ionic contamination testing only became routine later.

children.name: Wave-soldering machine
children.description: A conveyorised machine that drags the underside of the board through a standing wave of molten solder. Components are all inserted from the top so they point the same way, and the wave only ever touches leads and pads. It is why a 1983 line could put hundreds of sound joints on a board for the price of the solder.

facts.label: Preheat
facts.value: approx. 110-150 deg C in a tunnel before the wave

facts.label: Wave contact
facts.value: a few seconds, the length of the wave's contact length

children.name: Welded machine frame and shell
children.description: The pot, tunnel and conveyor sit in a welded steel frame that also carries the fume hood and the flux plumbing. It is a heavy, deliberately boring object: the machine is bought for its repeatability, not its elegance.

children.name: Structural steel sections
children.description: Mild steel angle and section from the arc or induction furnace. The mass of the frame is what keeps the wave flat while the pot runs.

children.name: Steel from iron ore and coke
children.description: Pig iron made in a blast furnace, refined in a basic oxygen furnace. The same ore, coke and limestone as the laminate press platen and the insertion machine bedplate.

children.name: Iron ore and metallurgical coke
children.description: Hematite or magnetite ore with coking coal. The two materials that make every steel machine on this floor, from the wave machine to the drill press.

children.name: Solder pot and wave former
children.description: A stainless or cast-iron pot holding tens to hundreds of kg of molten solder at roughly 250 deg C. Inside, a pump or a tilted paddle throws solder up against a forming dam, which spills over as a smooth standing wave. The pot is lined or plated because molten tin attacks iron.

facts.label: Pot metal
facts.value: cast iron with solder-resistant plating, or solid stainless

facts.label: Wave height
facts.value: a few millimetres above the pot lip, set by pump rate

children.name: Pot lining and dross skimmer
children.description: Dross collects as a floating raft that is dragged off the surface by a skimmer bar. Skipping this is the classic way to put oxide particles into every joint on the line, and it is why the skimmer is on the machine and not optional.

children.name: Stainless steel pot wall
children.description: The pot is stainless or plated cast iron, chosen because molten tin dissolves iron at 250 deg C. A bare iron pot would be eaten away in weeks, taking the wave geometry with it. This is the material decision that makes a wave machine a five-year purchase instead of a consumable.

children.name: Nickel in the stainless steel
children.description: Nickel is the component that makes stainless steel stainless: it forms a self-repairing chromium-oxide surface film that survives molten tin and most acids. The same nickel is the underplate beneath the gold on the board's edge contacts and the element in the burn-in oven's heating alloy.

children.name: Nickel ore
children.description: Pentlandite in nickel sulphide ore, or limonite in laterite, smelted and refined to metal.

children.name: Laterite or sulphide ore body
children.description: A weathered or igneous concentration of nickel minerals, mined open pit or underground and concentrated before the smelter. The last rock in a chain that began as the lining of a solder pot.

children.name: Drag-free twin-wave design
children.description: A single long wave exerts a strong forward drag on the board, which tears fine-pitch parts sideways and is the mechanical reason wave soldering lost to through-hole reflow. A twin-wave machine uses a main wave plus a smaller, faster secondary wave, or a double-peak former, that cuts the drag while still filling holes. Any serious 1983 machine had some version of this.
children.note: The same problem, later made worse by lead-free's higher melting point, is what pushed through-hole assembly off wave soldering onto selective solder.

children.name: Preheat tunnel
children.description: An oven before the wave that brings the whole board to roughly 120 deg C so the thermal shock of hitting 250 deg C solder is spread out. It also drives off moisture, which would otherwise spit solder out of the holes as the board hits the wave.

children.name: Recirculating hot-air preheat
children.description: Preheating is by moving air or radiant tubes, with the zone held below the solder melting point so nothing melts early. Too little preheat gives thermally shocked joints; too much dries the resin and lifts pads off the laminate.
children.note: A board full of large electrolytics takes a long time to come through, and preheater capacity is usually what sets the conveyor speed for the whole line.

children.name: Flux foamer
children.description: Just before the wave, a bank of porous stone immersed in rosin flux bubbles air through it and lays a thin, even, pre-activated film on the board's underside. Foaming gives uniform coverage a spray or brush never does, and it is where the smell of boiling pine on a board line comes from.

children.name: Sintered porous stone
children.description: A sintered polyethylene or polyurethane stone whose pore size is chosen to bubble air finely through the flux. It clogs with crystallised flux and has to be soaked out on a schedule.

children.name: Conveyor chain and fixtures
children.description: A stainless or phenolic chain carries boards through the machine, held by their edge in fixtures spaced along the chain. Chain pitch and fixture design, not the pump, set the real throughput. The fixtures were often the board's own edge, which is one reason board edge quality was a production concern.

children.name: Nitrogen blanket over the pot
children.description: Many machines piped nitrogen over the solder surface to keep the oxide skin thin and stop dross forming. It also stops the skin from insulating the pot from the wave, which makes the wave itself erratic.
children.note: Cheaper machines ran open to air and simply lived with the dross.

children.name: Cooling zone
children.description: After the wave, boards sit in moving hot air before leaving the machine. Hot air rather than cold, because chilling a freshly soldered joint around a large thermal-mass lead is how you get a cracked solder fillet.

children.name: Spares pot and solder return
children.description: A small pot under the wave catches solder running off the ends, which is then returned to the main pot. Recycling saves tin and, more importantly, stops the pot chemistry from drifting toward copper contamination.

children.name: The wave-soldering profile
children.description: The machine is set by five numbers together: pot temperature, conveyor speed, preheat temperature, preheat time, and flux concentration. Get them wrong in a specific way and you get a specific, diagnosable defect.

children.name: Why preheat sets joint quality
children.description: A joint cools from 250 deg C to 183 deg C in about a second. If the board and the lead start cold, the joint solidifies from the outside inward and you get the dull, grainy, poorly wetted fillet a line inspector rejects. Starting at 120 deg C lets the alloy flow properly before it freezes, which is the entire point of the preheat tunnel.

children.name: Heavy leads set the slowest joint
children.description: Large thermal-mass leads, such as the big axial electrolytic or the tabbed regulator, heat far more slowly than the solder around them. The line compensates by running the conveyor slowly enough that the solder stays molten until the lead is hot, which in turn slows every board on the machine.
children.note: This is why the big electrolytics are among the joints most often hand-touched after the wave, and why the instruction to check them existed at all.

children.name: What the joint is actually made of
children.description: Solder does not merely sit on a pad, it reacts with it. Within seconds of contact, tin and copper fuse at the surface into a hard intermetallic, which grows over time and eventually turns brittle and cracks. That is the origin of solder fatigue, and it explains why a leaded joint is forgiving and a lead-free one is not.

children.name: Copper-tin intermetallic growth
children.description: Cu6Sn5 forms at the pad surface and is the actual metallurgical bond holding the joint. It is hard and brittle, and its growth is limited by diffusion through itself, which is why higher-temperature solders containing silver or gold exist: to slow the reaction at the pad.

children.name: Named defects and what causes them
children.description: Dull grainy joints mean a dirty pad or too little preheat. Dry joints and unfilled holes mean a hole too tight for the lead or a wave too slow. Solder balls and spatter mean moisture in the board. Bridging between fine pads means too much flux, a pot too hot, or a wave too shallow. Blowholes in the joint mean damp.
children.note: This is the diagnostic vocabulary a line supervisor used in 1983, and it has barely changed since.

children.name: Hand soldering on the line
children.description: Soldering iron, solder wire and pliers on a bench under a smoke extraction arm. Used for the connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers, the big electrolytics and every joint the inspector rejected. A small minority of joints, but where the line rejects come from too.

facts.label: Tip material
facts.value: copper, often plated so it does not dissolve away

children.note: A small hand-held solder pot or a solder fountain was used for the fuse clips and heavy connector leads where a wave cannot reach.

children.name: Soldering iron and tip
children.description: A nichrome or cartridge heater in a barrel with a replaceable copper tip. The tip has to be kept tinned; a dry tip oxidises and then stops transferring heat at all, which is the real reason beginners conclude solder will not melt on a joint.

children.name: Copper tip material
children.description: Oxygen-free copper for heat transfer, sometimes plated. Copper dissolves into molten tin if left sitting in the pot, so tips were changed once they had thinned noticeably.

children.name: Fume extraction
children.description: An arm or hood over the bench draws off the flux smoke. The smoke is resin vapour, not tin vapour, but it is unpleasant and it is the reason every solder bench in 1983 had a hood over it.

children.name: Connectors, fuse clips and heavy joints
children.description: The parts that cannot simply be taken through the wave in the usual way: the D-sub and DIN connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers and the large electrolytics. These were soldered by hand, sometimes with a second iron used as a heat sink, and sometimes with a small solder pot.

children.name: Soldering with the connector already fitted
children.description: The board-mount connectors on the C64 mainboard are right-angle types with solder tails projecting out of the back of the shell. They were soldered from the underside with the shell already in place, which means a short working time and a hot iron in a cramped space.
children.note: The prevalence of resoldered connector joints on surviving C64 boards, decades later, is decent evidence that these joints were marginal from the start.

children.name: Bridging between connector pins
children.description: A D-sub or DIN connector has pins close enough that molten solder wicks along a pin and jumps the gap to the next pad, and inside a shell the bridge cannot be seen happening. The countermeasures in 1983 were flux plus a steady iron, then a probe and rework iron to break the bridge.
children.note: Modern lead-free practice would drag a solder bead along the pins to wick off the excess and, failing that, use a solder pot.

children.name: Two-iron technique for heavy joints
children.description: One iron on the joint and one on the lead keeps the lead at temperature while the solder melts, so the solder actually wets the lead instead of freezing a cold slug around it. Slower per joint, but the only way to get a sound joint onto a big thermal-mass part.

roots.name: Populating, cleaning and finishing the C64 mainboard
roots.description: What happens between the bare board and the tested machine. Components are inserted, a few hand-fitted wires and jumpers are added, the board is soldered, cleaned, shielded and screwed into the case. On this board the whole operation is through-hole and hand-and-machine insertion: there is no surface-mount reflow anywhere in the C64 mainboard assembly.
roots.note: Commodore specifically laid this board out for automated insertion, which cost them their Japanese assembly line and forced production into Hong Kong. The design decision to use DIP sockets rather than soldering the chips directly is a serviceability choice: it made field replacement possible, and it roughly doubled the number of joints on the board.

children.name: Component insertion
children.description: Every part goes into the board from the top. Because there are no vias and no bottom-side components, the whole machine is one-sided: one operator can see every joint from the solder side and there is no second-side insertion operation at all.

children.name: Insertion pitch set for the machine
children.description: Component spacing on this board was dictated by the insertion machine rather than by the circuit designer, which is exactly the argument Commodore had with its Japanese plant and lost. The same board could not be hand-inserted efficiently and machine-inserted efficiently at once.
children.note: The IEEE Spectrum account of the C64's design case history states the board was laid out for automated insertion and production was moved to a Hong Kong plant that had the automated tools.

children.name: Insertion engine and its cycle time
children.description: A machine with a magazine per part type picks a part, leads it to the right hole and pushes it in, typically in 0.3-0.6 s per component. On a board of about 90 parts that is roughly half a minute of machine time, which is why insertion engines paid for themselves on volume this high.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: the machine cannot compensate for a bent lead, so lead forming matters

children.name: Machine frame and bedplate
children.description: A cast-iron or welded steel bed with a linear axis and a vertical insertion head. The bedplate's flatness is the limit on how accurately a lead can be placed in a hole.

children.name: Cast iron machine base
children.description: Grey cast iron, machined flat. The same material and the same blast-furnace iron ore as the laminate press platen; machine tool bases have been cast iron for a century for the same reason.

children.name: Blast-furnace iron ore
children.description: Hematite or magnetite reduced with coke in a blast furnace. The industrial floor under this whole subsystem is iron ore and metallurgical coke.

children.name: Iron ore body
children.description: A concentration of iron oxides, mined open pit or underground, crushed, concentrated and sintered before the furnace.

children.name: Metallurgical coke
children.description: Baked coal, the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace and the source of its carbon monoxide.

children.name: Coal seam
children.description: Bituminous coal mined from a seam, crushed and carbonised in coke ovens. Diggable rock.

children.name: Part magazines and vibratory feed
children.description: Radial magazines shake components down a track to a pick head. Cut, formed axial leads are the hardest part to feed; resistors and capacitors with wide leads feed easily.
children.note: Failure of vibratory feeding, not of the machine itself, was the usual reason a line stopped on a board full of axial parts.

children.name: Insertion fixture and board handling
children.description: The board is held in a jig with locating pins while components go in, and the same family of jig carries the board through the wave and into test. Every fixture on the line solves the same problem: the board has to land in exactly one position, every time.

children.name: Fixture steel plate
children.description: Machined mild steel with hardened locating pins. The same blast-furnace iron ore and coke as every other machine tool on this floor.

children.name: Manual insertion and bench work
children.description: Everything the machine could not do: the fuse clips, the connectors, the small-signal parts in awkward places, the wire jumpers. Operators sat at the line with a board in a fixture and worked down a traveler's list of parts.
children.note: Mixed human-and-machine insertion on one board is a recipe for a component inserted twice or missed entirely, so the line had a checking station: a verifier that confirms every part is present and seated before the board goes into the wave.

children.name: Axial and radial lead forming
children.description: Axial parts are cut to length and formed to a right angle or left-right offsets so they drop into a fixed hole pitch. Radial parts are spread to the lead spacing of the board. The forms are set in the machine and are a real cost: a wrong form is a board that will not insert.

facts.label: Formed at
facts.value: the component maker or the insertion machine, not by hand on the line

facts.label: Radial pitch
facts.value: matched to the board hole pitch, often 0.1 in or 0.2 in

children.note: Modern practice forms nothing and mounts surface-mount parts; lead-formed axial parts are essentially gone from new consumer hardware.

children.name: DIP sockets as the C64's serviceability choice
children.description: This is the single most underappreciated decision on the board. The C64 sockets its integrated circuits rather than soldering them directly. It means any chip can be swapped in the field, and it means the number of joints roughly doubles, because each socket has two contacts per pin on each side.

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: roughly doubles the joint count and adds a failure mode of its own

children.note: The cost of a socketed chip is not just the socket money: it is four joints per pin where the original designer wanted one, and it is the reason C64 boards need so much rosin flux and so much cleaning. Commodore chose sockets because a home computer with unfield-serviceable ROMs or SID chips would generate warranty returns.

children.name: Resistors and the resistor networks
children.description: The board is full of small carbon-film resistors, some laid down as axial parts and some consolidated into resistor networks to save board area. The C64 is a good example of the 1980s trend toward integrating discrete resistors into single packages.

children.name: Resistor networks and hybrid packs
children.description: Several resistors in one small package with a common connection, replacing a handful of separate parts and their board area. The C64's data-line resistors are a good example of the era's move toward integration.
children.note: The exact part numbers and manufacturers of the C64's resistor networks vary by revision and have not been verified here; the practice itself is well attested for this period.

children.name: Carbon-film resistor element
children.description: A thin ceramic substrate coated with a semiconducting carbon film, trimmed to value. The resistor is the most numerous single part on the whole board.
children.note: Manufactured from petroleum-derived organics on a ceramic substrate; the materials detail is owned by the passives subsystem.

children.name: Wire jumpers and configuration links
children.description: Because the board has no vias, the few places where a connection must cross between the two copper layers with no component to do it are bridged with a short tinned copper wire, hand-fitted into two holes and hand-soldered. These are the E1 and E2 links on the 250407 layout.

facts.label: Fitted
facts.value: by hand, after the wave soldering

children.note: These are visible on the bottom of the finished board and are now a small collector's item in their own right. A modern board would put a via or a 0-ohm resistor there instead.

children.name: Tinned single-core jumper wire
children.description: A short length of fine tinned copper wire, cut and formed to the two holes, fitted and soldered by hand. It is the mechanical ancestor of the jumper link on every later board.
children.note: Modern equivalents are 0-ohm resistors, jumper pins, or just a via. None of those were on this board.

children.name: Connector and ribbon soldering
children.description: The edge-connector slots, the D-sub and DIN connectors, the fuse clips and the keyboard ribbon interface are all fitted and soldered by hand, because a conveyorised wave cannot hold them. This is a long bench task and a common source of rejects.
children.note: The keyboard connection on this board uses a flat ribbon; it is a delicate soldered joint and a classic failure point on surviving machines.

children.name: Reflow and surface-mount: not on this board
children.description: It is worth being explicit that the C64 mainboard has no surface-mount parts and no reflow step. Everything is through-hole, everything is either waved or hand-soldered. Reflow ovens were already known in 1983 but were used for flat-pack IC packages and for the small daughterboards, not for the main logic board.
children.note: A tree that claims reflow of the C64 mainboard is wrong. Modern boards are dominated by reflow; this one is not.

children.name: The RF modulator as a separate daughterboard
children.description: The C64's analogue RF modulator is a small separate board, not part of the main logic board, and in early machines it sits on the mainboard. Its construction and any SMT content belong to that module, not to this through-hole assembly.
children.note: Its SMT content, if any, has not been verified here.

children.name: Cleaning after soldering
children.description: Rosin flux leaves a sticky, slightly conductive film. The board is washed, historically in a solvent or detergent wash, sometimes with a little ultrasonic, then dried. The film matters: rosin is hygroscopic and mildly acidic, and in humid climates it slowly corrodes the board.

facts.label: Consequence if skipped
facts.value: surface leakage and, over years, corrosion

children.note: Cleaning was the step Commodore was known to skip or rush, which is a large part of why so many forty-year-old C64 boards show corrosion and leakage damage. Modern production uses deionised water and a resinous no-clean flux instead.

children.name: Conformal coating
children.description: A thin insulating coating over the assembled board to keep moisture and contaminants off the copper. The C64 mainboard was not conformally coated.
children.note: Conformal coating existed in 1983 for military and automotive work and was increasingly common in commercial electronics, but not for a home computer in a dry indoor case. If the tree you are building has conformal coating on the C64 mainboard, it is over-modelled.

children.name: EMI shield bonding
children.description: The metal shield around the video and audio circuitry is bonded to the board's ground so that the enclosure is actually part of the ground return. Without a real bond the shield picks up the very signals it is there to contain.

children.name: Shield lug and solder bond
children.description: A small tab on the shield is soldered to a ground pad or held by a screw into a plated hole, giving the enclosure a low-impedance path to the board's ground pour.
children.note: A through-hole into which a shield screw goes, or a soldered tab; the C64 used a combination, and the shield-to-board bond is one of the joints most often disturbed by owners.

children.name: The VIC-II heat-sink tab
children.description: A metal tab welded inside the shield lid pressed against the top of the video chip package, so the shield doubled as a heat sink for the chip that dissipated about 1.5 W. This was a deliberate design fix for a real heat problem, not a later addition.
children.note: The design history explicitly describes this tab being welded to the shield lid so the enclosure became a heat sink. It is a nice example of the enclosure, the ground return and the thermal path being one part.

children.name: Board-level rework and repair
children.description: Bad joints are reworked on the line: the joint is reflowed with an iron, the part is replaced, and a full set of consumable tips is kept to do it. Commodore's own engineering position was famously to ship rather than to hold back, which shows up here as rework being a normal, high-volume operation rather than an exception.
children.note: The engineering team's stated culture was that if a product worked it shipped, and that quality control was not coming close enough to where it should have been. That is visible in this subsystem as rework rather than scrap.

children.name: Volume and yield reality of the line
children.description: Commodore sold on the order of two million C64s a year at the 1983-84 peak, on a production cost that started near 130 dollars and fell as volume rose. Every board here was one of millions per year through the same line. Boards were made in Hong Kong, and in the first year of production at Kentron in Japan, which is where the 1982-83 units came from.

facts.label: Peak annual output
facts.value: roughly 2-2.5 million units a year around 1984

facts.label: Board yield
facts.value: high; a two-layer no-via board has few failure modes

children.note: The 1982-83 units were built at Kentron in Ina, Japan under Commodore Japan Limited, and the boards were made in Hong Kong. Whether Commodore ever had its own in-house PCB etching line is not established; the engineering account says the boards were made in Hong Kong, which implies an outside fabricator rather than a Commodore plant.

roots.name: Factory test of the C64 mainboard and machine
roots.description: How a populated C64 board was proved working before it left the factory. Electrical test on the bare board, then a functional test that boots the machine from a diagnostic ROM in the cartridge port and checks it against a monitor and a test cradle, then burn-in, then final test and packing. The practice was mostly manual, and Commodore's own engineers admitted it was thinner than it should have been.

facts.label: Stages
facts.value: bare-board electrical test, functional test, burn-in, final test

facts.label: Test ROM
facts.value: a diagnostic ROM run from the cartridge port

facts.label: Display check
facts.value: the machine's own video output viewed on a test monitor

roots.note: There are documented examples of new C64 machines shipping with cut traces, and a software developer's account of opening brand-new machines and finding them. That is the honest backdrop to this branch: it describes what was actually done, not what a modern line would do.

children.name: In-circuit electrical test
children.description: A bare populated board is checked electrically before it is ever plugged into a machine. The point is to catch a missing component, a shorted pad or a broken trace while it is still trivially fixable.

children.name: Bed-of-nails fixture
children.description: The board is pressed down onto a fixture whose probes touch every node of interest, so the tester can measure each net without a probe being placed by hand. On a board with no vias and only DIP footprints, the fixture is comparatively simple to design and to wire.

children.name: Spring probe pins
children.description: Small hardened probes on a sprung wire that survive repeated thousands of insertions. The fixture pinout has to be cut specifically for the board artwork, which is why fixtures were an expensive per-part-number investment.

children.name: Probe wire
children.description: Fine gold-plated or beryllium-copper wire drawn to a small diameter and formed into a sprung pin. Beryllium copper is used because it takes a permanent set and keeps its spring force after millions of cycles.

children.name: Copper (and beryllium) in the probe
children.description: The probe wire is copper alloy, drawing on the same copper supply as the board foil itself and the wave-solder pot. Copper is traced from cathode to concentrate by the metals subsystem.

children.name: Continuity, resistance and short detection
children.description: The tester looks for opens in the artwork and for shorts between nets that should be isolated, and on some fixtures measures absolute values. On a simple two-layer board with no vias, continuity checking is very nearly the whole job.
children.note: A modern flying-probe or X-ray system would do this without a custom fixture; in 1983 the bed of nails was the economical choice at volume.

children.name: Component-presence and seating check
children.description: Checking that the right part is in the right place is a distinct and important test on a board with thirty sockets and a hundred passive parts. A missing, reversed or half-seated socketed IC is the single most common fault on any 1980s logic board.
children.note: Verifiers that push each socket to confirm its pins are actually in the hole were in use in this era, alongside visual and continuity checks.

children.name: The tester itself
children.description: A rack of switching electronics driving the fixture, with a go or no-go readout and a reject bin. It is ordinary 1980s digital test equipment: a small computer, a relay matrix and a display, all built from the same logic families the C64 itself uses.

children.name: Functional test with a test ROM
children.description: The populated board is mounted in a test cradle with a power supply and a monitor, and the machine proves itself by running a diagnostic program from the cartridge port. This exercises the real boot path: CPU, ROM, RAM, character ROM, VIC, SID and the I/O chips, all in the configuration they will ship in.

facts.label: Test medium
facts.value: a diagnostic ROM in the cartridge port

facts.label: What it proves
facts.value: the machine can reach its own boot ROM and produce a correct picture and sound

children.note: Using the cartridge port as the test-vector delivery mechanism is an elegant piece of period engineering: no extra fixture hardware, and it tests the bus the machine actually uses.

children.name: Diagnostic and dead-test ROM
children.description: A small EPROM in a cartridge shell which, on power-up, prints a screenful of named tests and runs each one, reporting RAM, ROM and video faults by pattern rather than by instrument. The operator's job is to look at the picture and read the verdict.

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: no instruments needed; the machine tests itself and says so

children.note: These test ROMs were so successful that Commodore later sold the same idea to the public as the Dead Test cartridge, which is why they are so well documented today.

children.name: Test cradle
children.description: A jig that holds the board, presents a regulated 5 V and 12 V, routes the video and audio outputs to a monitor and speaker, and presents the cartridge and edge connectors. Several cradles were usually in line so inspectors could work in parallel.

children.name: Cradle body and fixture plate
children.description: A machined plate with locating pins that hold the board in exactly one position, mounted on a steel frame with the electronics below. Every fixture on the line has this same problem: the board has to land in the same place every time, and the pins are what guarantee it.

children.name: Fixture steel
children.description: Mild steel plate, machined and hardened at the locating pins so they do not wear out of tolerance. The same blast-furnace iron ore and coke as every other machine tool on this floor.

children.name: Iron ore and coke
children.description: Hematite or magnetite ore with coking coal, the two materials that make every steel jig on the line.

children.name: Coal seam
children.description: Bituminous coal mined from a seam, crushed and carbonised in coke ovens. A dug rock.

children.name: Test power supply
children.description: A regulated supply with a current limit so a shorted board does not destroy it. The C64's 5 V and 12 V came from its external supply, so the factory had to prove both the board and that supply; testing the PSU itself belongs to the power branch of this tree.

children.name: Keyboard and ribbon test
children.description: Because the keyboard connects to the mainboard through a soldered ribbon on this design, the functional test has to cover that joint: every key is checked, which is a simultaneous test of the connector, the ribbon, the keyboard matrix and the CPU's scanning routine.

children.name: CRT display test
children.description: The machine's own composite video output is fed to a test monitor and the inspector reads the picture. Nothing instruments this: the pass criterion is that the picture is correct, which means the human being in the loop is doing the measuring.

facts.label: What is checked
facts.value: a correct picture and sound: colours, borders, sprites, cursor

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: the human eye, plus a monitor

children.note: The engineering team said outright that testing colour quality automatically was effectively impossible, and that line workers were told to adjust a colour control until they saw colour. Several thousand machines shipped with garish colours as a result, and the instruction itself was the cause.

children.name: Test monitor
children.description: A small composite monochrome monitor, or a colour television, used as the reference picture. Each is a cathode-ray tube: drawn glass envelope, phosphor coating, deflection yoke and a high-voltage supply.

children.name: Shadow mask
children.description: A perforated steel sheet just behind the phosphor screen that makes each phosphor dot land on its own gun. It is made from Invar, a nickel-iron alloy whose thermal expansion is almost zero, so the mask does not move as the tube warms up.

children.name: Invar (nickel-iron)
children.description: About 36 % nickel in iron, notable for expanding almost not at all between 0 and 200 deg C. Nickel comes from sulphide ore or laterite, iron from iron ore.
children.note: Invar is the classic example of an alloy whose whole point is a property, not a strength.

children.name: Burn-in
children.description: Finished machines are powered up under load, often at elevated temperature, for an extended period. This was originally to weed out infant-mortality failures in the custom chips, which is exactly where the C64's problems were, and it is why there had to be a diagnostic ROM that could run unattended.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: catch early-life failures, especially in the custom chips

facts.label: Method
facts.value: machines run in racks, often warm, sometimes cycling

children.name: Burn-in oven or rack
children.description: A room or cabinet holding powered machines on racks, warmed to speed up failure. Heat is the cheap accelerator of every silicon and soldering defect there is, which is why burn-in exists at all.

children.name: Heating element (nichrome)
children.description: The resistance wire in the oven heater, an alloy of nickel and chromium that resists oxidation at red heat.

children.name: Nickel
children.description: The main constituent of the heating alloy, and also the underplate under the gold on the board's edge contacts. Nickel comes from sulphide ore, and later heavily from laterite.

children.name: Nickel ore (sulphide or laterite)
children.description: Pentlandite in nickel sulphide ore, or limonite in laterite. Smelted, refined and electrolytically won to metal. Diggable rock.

children.name: Laterite or sulphide ore body
children.description: A weathered or igneous concentration of nickel minerals, mined by open pit or underground and concentrated before the smelter.

children.name: Chromium
children.description: The second constituent of nichrome, from chromite ore. It is also the wear-resist plating on cutting tools and a constituent of the stainless steel used all over this factory.

children.name: Chromite ore
children.description: Iron chromium oxide, smelted to ferrochrome. Diggable rock.

children.name: Burn-in rack
children.description: A steel frame carrying a shelf of machines, with ventilation so the heat is actually reaching them. Racks were moved in and out of the oven on a schedule, which is a large amount of manual handling for what looks like a passive wait.

children.name: Unattended running
children.description: The diagnostic ROM is left to run so a machine that fails on its own gives a visible failure, freeing the line from one operator per machine. This is why the dead-test ROM's pattern output mattered as much as its pass or fail verdict.

children.name: Final test and packing
children.description: A last pass over the complete machine in its case: keyboard, control ports, serial port and a final power-on. Surviving machines are packed with the cord and the manual for shipment.

children.name: Control and serial port check
children.description: The two control ports and the serial port are exercised with known-good peripherals or loopback plugs. These are the connectors most often left untested on a line that was under pressure, and it is where the documented field failures of this era cluster.

children.name: Packing for shipment
children.description: The machine, cord and manual go into a carton, typically corrugated board with a printed outer. The packaging branch has its own industrial chemistry; this node marks only where the tested board leaves the factory.

roots.name: Phototooling: how C64 copper artwork became an etched board
roots.description: The chain that turns a board database into a resist image. The 250407 artwork is number 251137. It was drawn on a design workstation, reduced to aperture-table plot files, plotted onto photographic film at a jobbing house, developed, checked on a test coupon, and used as the mask that prints the board's dry-film resist before etching.

facts.label: Layers plotted
facts.value: 2 copper, plus solder mask and legend

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: vacuum-frame contact exposure of the artwork film onto dry film

roots.note: Modern practice is direct imaging from the CAM data with no film at all. The film phototooling described here is how the board in the machine was actually made.

children.name: The board database on the design system
children.description: In 1983 the layout lived on the CAD vendor's own workstation, not in a modern repository. Traces, pads, components and drill data were edited on the machine and periodically written out as plot files on tape or floppy. Copying it to the jobbing house was a physical act of transporting magnetic media.

children.name: CAD workstation
children.description: A dedicated 16-bit microcomputer or small minicomputer with its own storage, a high-resolution monochrome display, and often a pen plotter and a digitizer on the desk. The digitizer mattered as much as the plotter: designers drew and revised artwork on mylar overlays and digitised the changes back into the database.
children.note: Interactive PCB CAD in the 1980s was a commercial market dominated by a handful of vendors. The C64 layout predates every open format and tool used today.

children.name: Monochrome CRT display
children.description: A high-resolution green or white phosphor CRT on which the layout was examined trace by trace. The glass envelope, the phosphor coating and the shadow mask are all thin-film processes on a drawn glass bulb.
children.note: This is a designer's tooling CRT, not the machine's own video output, which is a separate branch of this tree.

children.name: CRT envelope glass
children.description: The bulb is soda-lime glass formed on a glass lathe from the same kind of batch as the reinforcing cloth: silica sand plus limestone plus alkali. A design workstation's screen is a small consumer item, but it is the terminal through which every copper trace of the board was examined.

children.name: Silica sand in the display glass
children.description: The main glass former in the CRT envelope, from the same washed and purified sand used for glass fibre. The glass chain of this tree has two exits to the same rock: reinforcing cloth and display glass.

children.name: Quartz sand deposit
children.description: Unconsolidated or friable sandstone worked for its sand. A dug mineral, and one of the few things in the whole phototooling chain that is not a petroleum product.

children.name: Plot-file storage media
children.description: Plot files and library data were written to nine-track tape, then to 8-inch floppy disks. The magnetic oxide on a thin polymer backing is the physical carrier the jobbing house receives, and a lost tape meant the whole panel waited.
children.note: This is the handover point between design and fabrication.

children.name: Backannotation from a drawn overlay
children.description: The designer taped mylar over the plotted printout, drew routing changes with a special pen, and passed the overlay through a digitizer that read the new lines and apertures back into the database. Slow, physical, and fiddly, and the reason routing history on boards of this era reads the way it does.
children.note: Some of the most awkward-looking copper on a 1983 board is the residue of this workflow: a routing decision made on a sheet of plastic and converted by an encoder.

children.name: Data reduction and CAM
children.description: The database is converted into per-layer plot files. This is where a net becomes copper, a component pin becomes a pad, and the drill hits are separated out. Errors here are replicated across a whole panel, which is why the step is done once, carefully, for hundreds of boards.

children.name: Netlist to routed copper
children.description: Connectivity becomes tracks per layer.
