On this two-layer board the routing problem is comparatively simple because there is no plane layer, but the ground return still has to be poured around the routing, and it is that pour which carries most of the finished board's signal integrity.
children.note: Autorouters handled most of the bulk in 1983 and a human cleaned up the critical nets. Hand pour plus hand cleanup is why the copper on a 1983 board looks the way it does.

children.name: Aperture table
children.description: Every distinct pad shape and track width is assigned an aperture in a table the plotter reads, so a 1.0 mm round pad and a 0.3 mm track are drawn as repeated simple shapes rather than as free curves. This aperture-table idea is the direct ancestor of the Gerber format, still the universal interchange format for board artwork today.
children.note: Gerber format was invented at this time to carry exactly this table, which is why it is still about apertures and flashes rather than geometry.

children.name: Drill file separation
children.description: The drill programme is split out from the copper data. On this board that is easy and low-risk because there are no vias, so the drill file is only component holes, mounting holes and the connector slots. A via-heavy board of the same era is where plot data and drill data were most often confused, and the result was a hole in the wrong place.
children.note: The no-via strategy simplifies CAM, not just drilling. It is one of the quieter efficiencies of the design.

children.name: Design rule checks
children.description: Automated checks for minimum track width, minimum spacing, pad-to-pad clearance and annular ring. On a board with no vias the annular-ring check has almost nothing to check, but spacing between fine pads on the IC footprints still matters.
children.note: A later twist on the C64 itself: owners of later board revisions found the layouts so tight that home repair needed bodge wires across the copper. That is a board designed to the limit.

children.name: Photoplotting the artwork film
children.description: The plot files drive a photoplotter that draws the copper artwork onto a transparent film. In 1983 these machines lived at the fabricator, not the design office, and were the company's most valuable single asset.

children.name: Electrostatic plotter
children.description: The dominant plotting technology of the era. A fine wire or shaped electrode is stepped across the film under computer control and a corona discharge exposes the emulsion wherever copper is wanted. Flatbed machines laid a film flat and exposed quickly, which is why they became the standard for two-sided work.
children.note: This is the technology lineage behind the Gerber format: Gerber Scientific commercialised these plotters and the aperture-table format that drove them, which is the format the industry still uses. Modern shops use laser plotters or direct imaging, but the format and its film are a direct inheritance.

children.name: Artwork film stock
children.description: A high-contrast, dimensionally stable photographic film that the plotter exposes and the shop develops into a finished mask. It must hold its geometry over a store door and be opaque where there is copper. The polymer base is the same class of polyester as the dry-film photoresist carrier.

children.name: Polyester film base (PET)
children.description: The dimensionally stable base the emulsion is coated on, made from polyethylene terephthalate. It is the reason a 1983 plotter film does not stretch and shift during handling, and it is the same polymer family as the photoresist carrier used on the board itself.

children.name: Ethylene glycol
children.description: One of the two feedstocks of PET, made by oxidising ethylene derived from ethylene. Ethylene comes from steam cracking of naphtha.

children.name: Ethylene
children.description: The two-carbon olefin from a steam cracker, parent of polyethylene and, with glycol, of polyester film.

children.name: Naphtha
children.description: The liquid petroleum fraction that is steam-cracked to make ethylene.

children.name: Crude oil
children.description: The hydrocarbon mixture from a reservoir, fractionated and cracked into the aromatics and olefins that make the film, the resist, the ink and the machine tools of this entire tree.

children.name: Petroleum reservoir
children.description: Porous rock holding crude under pressure, produced through steel casing into a gathering system. This is the bottom of the whole tree: everything on this branch that is not mineral is a refined version of this.

children.name: Pen plotter (older, slower)
children.description: A carriage carrying a light-sensitive pen draws the artwork directly on film or mylar. Simple and reliable, but slow, with real line-width variation, so it was being displaced by the electrostatic plotter through the early 1980s and by the laser plotter later.
children.note: Still used for check plots and for prototype single-layer boards well into the 1980s.

children.name: Laser plotter (arriving)
children.description: An argon-ion or, later, a diode laser writes the film or the photoresist directly. Sharper than corona discharge and faster, but in 1983 it was still being adopted and the electrostatic plotter was not yet history.
children.note: The last piece of 1980s phototooling equipment before direct imaging replaced film entirely in the 1990s.

children.name: Developing and fixing the film
children.description: The exposed film is developed, fixed, washed and dried before it can serve as a mask. The chemistry is ordinary silver-halide photographic processing, run as a short line of tanks.

children.name: Photographic developer (hydroquinone)
children.description: The film emulsion is silver halide; hydroquinone reduces the exposed grains to metallic silver, giving the opaque image that will block the resist. The reducing agent is itself an aromatic chemical made from benzene, so the mask chemistry is a petroleum chain like everything else in this branch.

children.name: Benzene-derived intermediates
children.description: Hydroquinone is made by dihydroxylating benzene. Benzene comes from the heavy naphtha fraction of crude oil, so the developer that draws the copper pattern is two refinery steps from crude.

children.name: Heavy naphtha
children.description: A mid-boiling petroleum fraction, solvent-extracted for benzene.

children.name: Crude oil
children.description: The unrefined petroleum the naphtha is cut from.

children.name: Petroleum reservoir
children.description: The sedimentary rock that holds it.

children.name: Fixer (ammonium thiosulfate)
children.description: The unexposed silver halide is dissolved away and the image made light-stable, so the film can be handled, stored and re-exposed without latent-image changes.
children.note: Thiosulfate chemistry is a sulfur chain, ultimately from sulfur or from sulphur dioxide off sulfide roasting, so it is a different mineral chain from the aromatic one.

children.name: Rephotography, the master, and the coupon
children.description: The plotted working film is rephotographed onto a higher-quality film to get a sharper, dimensionally stable master. Before a whole panel is committed, a test coupon is exposed and etched with every line width the panel uses, and the widths are measured. This is how a shop proves its process still holds tolerance.

facts.label: Coupon
facts.value: a small test board carrying every line width and pad size on the panel

facts.label: Check
facts.value: measure the narrowest trace on the panel under a measuring microscope

children.note: The coupon is the quiet heart of 1980s board making: a cheap, fast way to prove that the narrowest trace the designer asked for is still coming out, before a hundred boards are committed to it.

children.name: The artwork master
children.description: The film treated as the authoritative copy of the design, stored flat and handled by the edges. It is the board's master record, and losing it means paying for the panel again.

children.name: Printing the artwork onto the resist
children.description: The artwork film is laid against the exposed dry-film resist on the board and exposed in the vacuum frame. Where the film is clear, the resist hardens and resists the etch; where it is opaque, the resist stays soft and the copper beneath is etched away. This is the moment the phototooling chain finally touches the board, and every solder joint on the finished machine is located by this exposure.

children.name: Two-sided registration
children.description: The hard part of a two-sided board. The second side's artwork has to land on the copper to within a fraction of a millimetre, using alignment pins and a register mark. On this board it matters mainly for the mounting holes and the connector slots; on a via-heavy board it is what decides whether every barrel lands on its own pad.
children.note: Having no vias makes two-sided registration a far less critical operation than on a modern via-heavy board, one of the quieter payoffs of the layer-change-by-component-lead strategy.

children.name: Panelising the order
children.description: The board is one part out of a panel of identical boards nested in a sheet large enough for the process equipment. The panel gets tooling holes for registration and for the drill, and the boards are separated later. This is where the layout cost of an order is amortised, and why a two-layer panel in 1983 could hold a surprising number of boards.

children.name: Tooling and mouse-bite tabs
children.description: The nested boards are held by small perforated tabs, broken out by hand or by a router after the panel is finished. The tabs leave a characteristic rough edge on the board outline, which is visible on a 1983 board if you look at it.
